JPE1375 reduced IL-1β secretion by ~50% during monocyte stimulation with LPS+CC ( ). This effect was specific to IL-1β as JPE1375 had no impact on the production of tumor necrosis factor (TNF) or IL-10 ( ). While exposure of human monocytes to increasing amounts of LPS or CC induced, as expected, a proportional increase in cell death ( ), the in vitro priming and CC activation conditions used here did not affect cell viability and neither did addition of PMX53 or JPE1375 to cultures ( ). C5AR1 transcription and protein expression increased > 2-fold upon CC and LPS+CC exposure, while C5 and C5aR2 transcription and protein concentrations remained largely unchanged across activation conditions. We noticed, however, that CC-sensing, with and without LPS-priming, augmented intracellular C5a generation and C5aR1 protein expression ( and ). Moreover, while intracellular C5a pools and intracellular C5aR1 occupied largely distinct subcellular locations in resting monocytes, LPS+CC activation induced visibly increased colocalization of this receptor-ligand pair ( ). We also noted colocalization between C5aR1 and NLRP3 in resting and activated monocytes ( ), although the implication of this finding is currently unclear. Together, these findings indicate that CC-sensing in monocytes mobilizes and engages the C5 complosome and supports IL-1β production. We next assessed if our observations extended to macrophages as those represent the disease-driving cells in atherosclerotic lesions and other contexts of sterile inflammation. Indeed, human monocyte-derived macrophages (hMDM) also contained C5 and C5a stores, expressed the C5aRs in a pattern comparable to monocytes ( ), and displayed ~ 50% reduction in IL-1β secretion after LPS+CC activation upon selective intracellular C5aR1 blockage, without an effect on cell viability ( , and ). Importantly, when LPS-primed hMDM were exposed to monosodium urate (MSU) crystals, which generally evoke a similar NLRP3-dependent IL-1β response, we also observed a significant decrease of IL-1β secretion in the presence of the cell-permeable C5aR1 inhibitor ( ). These data indicate that intracellular C5aR1 activation may be a general feature during crystal-sensing in human myeloid cells. We next probed whether the C5 complosome induces caspase-8 activation, because this can drive IL-1β secretion ( , ). Exposure of hMDMs to E.coli induced caspase-8 activation whereas LPS priming and crystal-sensing did not ( ), suggesting that C5aR1 drives IL-1β generation independently of caspase-8. In line with the inhibitor-generated data, knock-down of C5aR1 or C5 by siRNA technique in hMDM ( ) diminished mature IL-1β secretion ( ) without impacting TNF or IL-10 production or cell viability ( and ) in LPS+CC-stimulated macrophages. Thus, inhibition of C5 receptor engagement also impairs IL1B gene transcription ( ). Importantly, under all activation conditions assessed, expression of genes encoding key NLRP3 inflammasome components, such as NLRP3 and ASC , or the major NLRP3 inflammasome target, CASP1 , was not changed ( ). However, higher doses of LPS augmented, as expected, NLRP3 gene expression ( ). Interestingly, the effects of C5aR1 blockade on in vitro -differentiated human M1 and M2 macrophages upon LPS activation was different from those observed in monocytes and non-differentiated macrophages ( and ). Freshly isolated monocytes expressed CFD and CFB at low levels and LPS priming significantly induced CFB (but not CFD ) levels ( ). Multiple cell plane (z-stack) analyses confirmed the presence of C3bBb and/or C3bBbC3b complexes within the cell’s interior ( ). FACS analyses of resting and CC-activated, permeabilized or non-permeabilized, monocytes indicated that the majority of C5 convertases formed under the cell membrane, but that a proportion of convertases also localized to the monocyte cell surface ( and ). It is currently not possible to discriminate between formation of C3 vs. C5 convertases as both are composed of the same proteins assembled in different proportions. Western blot analyses of non-activated and CC -ctivated monocytes further confirmed the generation of the active Bb fragment by monocytes ( ) and of FD protein (we were unable to determine whether cells contained the pro-form and/or the processed form of FD ( )) ( ). Western blot analyses of subcellular fractions of resting human monocytes confirmed co-localization of C3b, Bb, and FD with the cell membrane ( ). Surprisingly, however, we also observed the presence of C3b, FB, Bb, and FD on mitochondria and other, not further defined, organelles ( ). The reduction of FB expression ( , upper panel ) by siRNA led to a proportional decrease in IL-1β secretion by CC-exposed monocytes ( , lower panel ) but did not reduce TNF generation ( ), in line with our observation that intracellular C5a specifically drives IL-1β production. We next assessed the impact of a newly developed human FB inhibitor (cpFBinh) ( ) on the monocyte cell-intrinsic C5 system. This FB inhibitor is highly cell-permeable ( ) and hence potently inhibits both extra- and intracellular FB activity. To simplify the experimental set-up, we utilized high (100 ng/ml) LPS activation as strong toll-like receptor (TLR) 4 engagement drives both FB expression and IL-1β production. Activation of human monocytes in the presence of cpFBinh indeed reduced intracellular C5a generation by high LPS-stimulated monocytes ( ), which led to a concurrent decrease in their IL-1β production ( ). The addition of an antibody to FB that inhibits FB-driven convertase formation only on the cell surface had a limited effect on intracellular C5a generation and IL-1β production ( and ). Incubation of LPS-activated monocytes with the C5aR1 inhibitor JPE1375 in the presence of the cpFBinh did not further reduce IL-1β production ( ). Together, these data support that human monocytes harbor a fully cell-autonomous C5 activation system. They also indicate the requirement for intracellular FB and C5 convertase activity to enable C5aR1 engagement for IL-1β production in DAMP-sensing human monocytes. We noted C4 and C2 gene transcription as well as C4 and C2 protein expression in resting monocytes. Further, CC-sensing increased C4 protein expression ( and ). Western blot analyses of resting and activated human monocytes confirmed that C4 and C2 were present mostly in their processed active forms as C4b and C2b, respectively ( ). Also, and similarly to C3b, C4b was predominantly intracellularly localized, while a relatively large proportion of C2b was present on the cell surface ( and ). These observations suggest that monocytes may also support formation of intracellular classical pathway C3 and C5 convertases (C4bC2b and C4bC2bC3b), which warrants further exploration. Together, these data demonstrate the intracellular formation of the central serum complement activation hubs, the C3/C5 convertases, in human monocytes and suggest that intracellular inhibition of the alternative pathway C3/C5 convertase formation may be a means to modulate IL-1β production by myeloid cells during sterile inflammation. Western blots of sub-cellular fractions from resting human monocytes confirmed the presence of C5aR1 in the plasma membrane, the cytoplasm, mitochondria and other organelles, including lysosomes ( and ). Because of our previous finding that intracellular C5aR1 in T cells augments ROS production during Th1 induction ( ), we hypothesized that mitochondrial C5aR1 may impact mitochondrial activity, the principal source of ROS production in mammalian cells. C5aR1 was expressed on mitochondria in resting monocytes, specifically the outer mitochondrial membrane, as evidenced by co-localization with both a mitochondrial stain ( ) and with TOM20 ( ). This was confirmed by C5aR1 Immunogold staining and electron microscopy analyses of non-activated THP-1 cells, a human monocytic cell line ( ). We also observed colocalization of C5a with mitochondrial-expressed C5aR1 (mtC5aR1) ( ), indicating that C5a is targeted to mtC5aR1 and could exert biological effects on mitochondria. To probe whether mtC5aR1 can respond to ligand activation, isolated mitochondria were exposed to increasing amounts of serum-purified C5a ranging from 5 to 50 ng/ml (C5a amounts commonly found in circulation range from approximately 20 – 150 ng/ml). To obtain sufficient pure mitochondria, we utilized non-activated THP-1 cells. High purity of mitochondria in isolated sub-cellular fractions was confirmed by the absence of Ras-related protein Rab-11A (RAB11) and tubulin ( ). Addition of C5a to mitochondria evoked ROS production, a measure of mitochondrial activity, in a dose-dependent manner, and in a classic bell-shaped response profile characteristic of C5aR signaling elsewhere ( ) ( ). Collectively, these data indicate that mitochondria express a functional C5aR1 that responds to specific C5a ligand engagement and induces ROS production via G protein coupling. We next assessed the downstream signaling pathway(s) recruited by liganded mtC5aR1 in monocytes and macrophages. GPCR signaling, including that of C5aR1, has been studied traditionally with a focus on plasma membrane-embedded receptors. Nevertheless, GPCRs are also observed in cellular sub-compartments ( – ), where they can engage canonical signal transduction ( ). Constitutive activity of mitochondrial-associated ERK1/2 is a requirement for mitochondrial ATP generation. Surprisingly, diminished ATP did not trigger phosphorylation of mitochondrial 5’ AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), which is typically observed when ATP concentrations drop ( ) ( , and ). Surprisingly, diminished ATP did not trigger phosphorylation of mitochondrial 5’ AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), which is typically observed when ATP concentrations drop ( ) ( , and ). When faced with limited ATP provision from respiration, cells can generate ATP through glycolysis to meet the bioenergetic demands of effector responses. In fact, high glycolytic activity is a feature of pro-inflammatory monocytes and macrophages ( ). We thus hypothesized that mtC5aR1 activation may result in metabolic shift and assessed glycolysis and OXPHOS in human resting and LPS+CC-activated monocytes in the presence or absence of JPE1375. LPS+CC activation significantly augmented glycolysis vs. coupled (ATP-producing) respiration ( ). This was dependent on mtC5aR1 as the effect was lost upon intracellular C5aR1 inhibition ( ). Interestingly, although intracellular C5aR1-mediated signals are required for nigericin-driven IL-1β production, nigericin induced distinct metabolic profiles, which seem rather potentiated by mtC5aR1 inhibition, compared to those driven by sensing crystals, ( ). Thus, metabolic adaptations initiated by intracellular mtC5aR1 seem adjusted according to the nature of the sensed DAMP. The observed reduction in glycolysis upon intracellular C5aR1 inhibition was not due to limitation of glucose flux as neither expression of the glucose transporter GLUT1 ( and ) nor the uptake of glucose was reduced ( and ). As expected, inhibition of glycolysis by 2-DG strongly reduced IL-1β production by human LPS+CC-activated monocytes with or without JPE1375 addition to cultures ( ) ( and ). Hexokinases (HK) I and II are initial enzymes of glycolysis and catalyze generation of glucose-6-phoshate (G6P) from glucose. HKs can be mitochondria-associated where they control VDAC channel opening, mitochondrial integrity, cell survival and NLRP3 activation ( , ). Silencing of C5AR1 in human macrophages reduced the release of HKI from mitochondria in resting and in LPS+CC-activated cells, presumably due to reduced glycolysis ( ) ( and ). Together, these data indicate that inhibition of intracellular C5aR1 does not impair glucose uptake and initiation of glycolytic flux but rather directly impacts mitochondrial activity. Consistent with this, while the expression of C5aR1 on mitochondria did not change during priming or crystal-sensing ( ), inhibition of mtC5aR1 function by JPE1375 affected mitochondrial mass and dynamics ( to ). Importantly, while high LPS doses normally induce mitochondrial mass (as a measure of biogenesis) in macrophages ( ) and ), the priming and CC-sensing conditions used here to evoke IL-1β production rather led to a decrease in mitochondrial mass ( and ). Pre-incubation of cells with JPE1375 had no effect on mitochondrial mass in activated cells but JPE1375 surprisingly increased mitochondrial biogenesis in resting cells ( and ). Assessment of mitochondrial morphology ( ) in CC-sensing THP-1 cells by confocal microscopy ( ) supported a role for the mtC5aR1 in directing mitochondrial dynamics. DISCUSSION Sustained complement activation, triggered by endogenous DAMPs or by non-infective irritants has long been identified as a driver of sterile inflammation underlying, for example, gout, kidney fibrosis, and atherosclerosis ( , , – ). C5aR1 is particularly relevant to sterile inflammation because activation of C5aR1 on endothelial cells during heightened complement activation induces an inflammatory state in these cells, while C5aR1 activation on innate immune cells fosters attachment to the inflamed endothelium, uptake of antigen, tissue infiltration and induction of a pro-inflammatory effector phenotype ( ). These events together sustain chronic pathologic tissue inflammation. Inflammation-driving C5aR1-mediated signals on myeloid cells are currently thought to solely originate from cell surface-expressed C5aR1. Here, we show that the C5aR1 is also present on mitochondria in monocytes and macrophages and that intracellular mtC5aR1 stimulation critically contributes to myeloid IL-1β responses underlying sterile inflammation. These data align well with previous observations that cyclodextrin promotes regression of atherosclerosis, at least in part, via reducing intrinsic complement activity in plaque-resident macrophages ( ). The unexpected role of intracellular C5 in driving mtC5aR1 signaling in myeloid cells may explain why reducing C5 activation in the plasma of patients with ACVD has not proven clinically beneficial ( ). Furthermore, a better understanding of the functions of complement in sterile chronic inflammation and specifically its role in IL-1β biology may help in developing alternate therapeutic strategies. Our studies demonstrated not only the broad importance of intracellular C5aR1 for DAMP sensing in several disease models, but also showed that mtC5aR1 signaling has non-uniform effects on cytokine production by monocytes and macrophages. For example, during thioglycolate-induced peritonitis, the macrophage cell-intrinsic C5 system restrained ROS and IL-1β production ( ) and enhanced TNF generation. Thus, the net outcome of mtC5aR1 stimulation on IL-1β production during sterile inflammation appears to be dependent on the integration of upstream, lateral, and downstream signals. These involve the sensing monocyte or macrophage sub-population, the nature and strength of the DAMP trigger (likely dictating the cellular C5a concentrations) and cross-engagement with other PRR sensor systems ( ). In fact, earlier studies utilizing global C5ar1 −/− mice and different pathogen dosages also noted that C5aR1 deficiency reduced mouse BMDM but increased peritoneal monocyte IL-1β production upon TLR4 activation in models of sepsis ( , ). The differences in the outcome of myeloid cell responses to mtC5aR1 engagement is likely due to distinct C5aR1 (or other complosome component) expression signatures among monocytes, macrophages and dendritic cells, as have been noted in both mice and humans ( – ), and/or to distinct metabolic sensors engaged ( ). For example, in human M2, but not M1, macrophages, ATP sensing is uncoupled from the NLRP3 inflammasome and IL-1β production is controlled by ROS and the cytoskeleton ( ). Accordingly, we also found IL-1β suppression only in M2, but not M1, macrophages upon mtC5aR1 blockade. Conversely, mtC5aR1 inhibition reduced IL-10 production in differentiated M1, but not M2, macrophages ( ). The latter finding probably explains the impact of C5aR1 inhibition on both IL-1β and IL-10 (and possibly also on the TNF pathway gene signature) of plaque-resident myeloid cells from the CVD patients, as the plaques harbor a mixture of M1 and M2 (and other) macrophage populations ( ). The identification of the C5aR1 as a mitochondrial modulator of ROS production and glycogenic vs. non-glycogenic ATP generation aligns with the emerging role of the complosome as orchestrator of basic biochemical and particularly metabolic reactions. Such non-canonical intracellular functions of complement are consistent with the fact that other ancient PRR systems are also involved in basic physiological processes of the cell ( , ). Conceptually, our findings are also in line with the fact that a large proportion of GPCRs (or receptors in general) operate at the cell surface and within intracellular compartments and that the location of their engagement may dictate the nature of signaling pathways induced ( ). Of note, C5aR1 does not contain a canonical mitochondrial targeting signal and the molecular mechanism directing C5aR1 subcellular trafficking is unknown, but may be an interesting area of future research. Of importance will also be to further define the diverse triggers and modes of mtC5aR1 engagement in vivo during sterile inflammation (for example, the response to apoptotic cell sensing) in more depth for potential therapeutic intervention. Here, we explored a model in which monocytes ingest CC and engage the C5-NLRP3 inflammasome axis rather rapidly to trigger IL-1β production. However, mtC5aR1 activity may also be engaged in a more gradual fashion: Western diet induces the accumulation of minimally modified (mmLDL) or oxidized (oxLDL) LDL in macrophage lysosomes over time, where they eventually form crystal ( ). chunks.content: Introduction Hip fractures represent a major public health issue and are the most severe yet common consequence of osteoporosis [ – ]. They account for a substantial loss of healthy life years, driven by high rates of complications, mortality, long-term disability, and loss of autonomy [ , , – ]. The rising incidence of hip fractures due to demographic aging is already imposing significant costs on healthcare systems worldwide [ , ]. Effective management of hip fractures is therefore a priority to reduce their burden on individuals, society and healthcare infrastructures. While many risk factors are well known, yet largely non-modifiable [ , ], timing of surgical intervention is a critical modifiable factor influencing patient outcomes. Timely surgery is essential to alleviate pain, enable early mobilization, and prevent complications, such as urinary tract infections (OR 0.57 [ ], 0.44 [ ]), pneumonia (OR 0.83 [ ]), congestive heart failure (OR 0.77 [ ]), delirium (0.47 [ , ]), pressure ulcers (OR 0.55 [ ]; 0.25 [ ]), deep vein thrombosis (OR 0.61 [ ]; OR 1.1/d [ ]). Furthermore, prolonged bedrest leads to muscular and systemic deconditioning [ ]. Conversely, delayed surgery is associated with longer hospital stays, higher complication rates, and increased mortality [ , , – ]. Current international guidelines recommend surgery within 24 to 48 h of hospital admission, with some advocating for even earlier intervention [ , – ]. However, the precise threshold for acceptable delay remains under debate, complicated by conflicting study results and logistical feasibility [ , , , , , , – ]. Importantly, evidence on the timing of surgery often overlooks distinctions between different hip fracture types - particularly trochanteric versus femoral neck fractures. These subtypes vary in anatomical location, treatment strategies, patient demographics, and clinical outcomes. Trochanteric fractures - being extracapsular – are associated with a higher primary blood loss than intracapsular femoral neck fractures [ ]. They are usually managed with closed reduction and intramedullary nailing, a procedure that is relatively fast, resource-efficient, and technically less demanding than arthroplasty [ , ]. In contrast, femoral neck fractures are intracapsular and commonly require internal fixation or hip arthroplasty. Patients with trochanteric fractures tend to be older, with lower baseline mobility and fitness, and have worse clinical outcomes including higher complication and mortality rates, as well as prolonged hospitalization and rehabilitation [ , – ]. Grouping both fracture types in research may obscure important fracture-specific insights – highlighting the need for more targeted research on the optimal timing of surgery, particularly for trochanteric fractures. A further complication lies in the challenge of performing hip fracture surgery during nighttime hours. Despite the urgency of timely intervention, overnight procedures raise safety concerns due to surgeon fatigue, reduced staffing, and slower workflows [ ]. These system-level barriers can undermine guideline adherence and make scheduling within the recommended timeframe difficult. Balancing the benefits of early surgery with the potential risks of nighttime operations remains a pressing issue, particularly as healthcare systems strive to optimize outcomes under constrained resources. Aim This study investigates the influence of preoperative delay and nighttime surgery on in-hospital complication and mortality rates in patients with trochanteric fractures. We hypothesize that surgery performed within 24 h improves outcomes, irrespective of whether it is performed during day- or nighttime. With the fracture-specific focus of this research, we seek to address the limitations of prior studies and contribute evidence regarding the optimal timing of surgery for trochanteric hip fractures. Our findings aim to guide clinical practice and improve outcome. Materials and methods Study design and setting We analyzed the data of patients with trochanteric femur fractures from the prospective surgical registry of the working group for quality assurance in surgery (“Arbeitsgemeinschaft für Qualitätssicherung in der Chirurgie” or AQC). The AQC is a voluntary association of physicians in Switzerland formed with the aim of evaluating the in-hospital outcomes of surgical patients. Since almost 30 years 166 departments/attending doctors contributed 2.1 million anonymized cases with the purpose of ensuring surgical quality in Switzerland [ ]. The database contains information about (a) the hospitalization and (b) the procedure(s). The diagnosis is coded according to the International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Edition (ICD-10) - a clinical cataloguing system developed by the World Health Organization (WHO) [ ]. Procedures are coded according to the Swiss operation classification ‘CHOP’ [ ]. Because only de-identified data from this national database was used, no institutional review board approval was required. Study subjects The inclusion criteria for the current study consisted of patients with the main diagnosis trochanteric femur fractures (ICD code S72.1) and main surgery by closed reduction and internal fixation (CRIF, CHOP code 79.15). Under the considerations of ICD and CHOP 9094 patients were elicited, 1910 cases were excluded due to missing data, especially the starting time of the surgery to ensure accurate timing analysis, leaving a total of 7184 patients with operatively treated trochanteric femur fractures between January 5th, 2001, and April 19th, 2024. Variables and outcome measures The following parameters from the AQC database were considered for this study: patient’s age, sex, American Society of Anaesthesiologists (ASA) physical status classification system score, type of insurance (statutory or private), surgeon class (senior attending, junior attending, resident), length of surgery in minutes, the occurrence of any complication (yes or no), length of hospital stay in days, and discharge status (home, rehabilitation clinic, nursing home, old people’s home, death, and others). Complication comprised general (e.g. pneumonia, renal dysfunction), intraoperative (e.g. iatrogenic fractures, tissue damage) or postoperative (e.g. bleeding, infection, malreduction). No standardized frailty scoring system was applied and the fractures were not subclassified according to severity. We categorized the patients according to the preoperative interval (less or more than 24 h) to evaluate the influence of surgical delay. For further analysis, we stratified the patients into two additional groups based on the time of surgery start: ‘DAY,’ for surgeries starting between 7:00 a.m. and 6:59 p.m., and ‘NIGHT,’ for surgeries starting between 7:00 p.m. and 6:59 am. The occurrence of any complication during the hospitalization was the primary outcome, whereas in-hospital mortality was the secondary outcome. Statistical analysis The data was downloaded from the AQC database using the AdjumedAnalyze software (Adjumed Services AG, Zurich, Switzerland). The statistical analysis was executed in SPSS version 29.0.2.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). The chi-square test was employed for analysis of the categorical data, presented as absolute numbers of patients and their corresponding percentages. An unpaired t-test was performed to compare the numerical data, presented as means ± standard deviation (SD). A p -value of < 0.05 was considered to indicate statistical significance. We utilized backward stepwise binary logistic regression as a statistical tool to explore and identify independent risk factors associated with the likelihood of any complication and death. ASA V and ASA I were excluded as predictors for mortality, since they were always associated (or not at all) with death. Results Study population A total of 7184 patients were included in the study. The mean age was 82 ± 11 years, the patients had predominantly a female sex (73%). An ASA score of II or III was recorded in 90% of patients, with 45% having ASA II and 45% ASA III, followed by ASA I with 6.3% and ASA IV with 2.9%. Statutory insurance covered 74% of the patients, and 42% of the surgeries were done by junior consultants, 30% by senior consultants, and 28% by residents. The length of surgery was 68 ± 39 min. The patients stayed 10 ± 6 days. After the hospital stay, 26% went home, 29% were discharged to a rehabilitation clinic, 15% to an old people’s home, and 19% to a nursing home (Table ). Preoperative delay of > 24 h Nine hundred and fifty patients (13%) received surgery after more than 24 h of hospitalization. These patients had similar age and sex as the group with a delay of less than 24 h, however, they had a significantly higher ASA score and a marginally greater coverage under statutory insurance. In the group with preoperative delay over 24 h, we observed a statistically significant difference in the length of surgery (70 ± 53 vs. 67 ± 37 min), occurrence of any complication (22% vs. 16%), and length of hospitalization (12 ± 7 vs. 10 ± 6 days). Also, patients were more often discharged to a nursing home (21% vs. 18%) or deceased (5.4% vs. 3.1%) and less often discharged home (24% vs. 26%) or to a rehabilitation clinic (28% vs. 30%) (Table ). Complications The overall complication rate was 17%. Surgery delayed beyond 24 h was associated with a 37.5% increase in the complication rate (22% vs. 16%). Binary logistic regression analysis identified delayed surgery > 24 h, an increased ASA score, male sex, higher age and longer surgery duration as significant risk factors for the occurrence of complications. (Table ) Hence, delayed surgery after 24 h was confirmed as an independent risk factor, indicating a 38% increased risk for the occurrence of any complication. Mortality The overall in-hospital

Binary logistic regression analysis identified delayed surgery > 24 h, an increased ASA score, male sex, higher age and longer surgery duration as significant risk factors for the occurrence of complications. (Table ) Hence, delayed surgery after 24 h was confirmed as an independent risk factor, indicating a 38% increased risk for the occurrence of any complication. Mortality The overall in-hospital mortality was 3.4%. Delayed surgery was significantly associated with a 74% increase in the mortality rate (5.4% vs. 3.1%), but not a significant predictor for mortality in regression analysis. Binary logistic regression identified complications and advancing age as significant risk factors for mortality (Table ). Daytime versus nighttime surgery Among 2406 patients, the exact starting time of the surgery was available. The complication rate was similar between the daytime and nighttime groups ( p = 0.263), and mortality rates were also not statistically different ( p = 0.15). Including this dichotomous parameter in the logistic regression, the timing of surgery was not retained in the final regression model (Table ). Discussion Key findings Our study contributes additional evidence to the ongoing debate, whether delayed surgery > 24 h or nighttime surgery starting between 7:00 p.m. and 6:59 am increases the in-hospital complication and mortality rate. In this nationwide retrospective cohort study (evidence level III), we analysed 7184 patients with trochanteric femur fractures treated with CRIF during an almost 24-year period. In our study, patients receiving early surgery within 24 h of admission showed a better in-hospital outcome. Patients undergoing delayed surgery had an increased complication rate (22% vs. 17%). Preoperative delay was found to be an independent risk factor for the occurrence of complications, alongside with an increased ASA score, male sex, higher age, and longer surgery duration. Delayed surgery was significantly associated with mortality (5.4% vs. 3.1%), but not a significant predictor for mortality in the regression analysis. Independent risk factors for mortality were higher ASA scores, the occurrence of any complication, male sex, and advancing age. Nighttime surgery was not associated with a higher complication or mortality rate, nor was it a significant risk factor in multivariate analysis. While the timing of hip fracture surgery has been studied extensively, fracture-type-specific analyses remain rare. Implications Our findings highlight the critical role of early surgery within 24 h of admission in reducing in-house complications, mortality and hospital stay, particularly for trochanteric femur fractures. Preoperative delay emerged as the most modifiable predictor of adverse outcomes. Surgical delay did not predict mortality independently, but the occurrence of any complication. Concerns about night-time surgery should not justify delays. Instead, strategic prioritization can optimize resource allocation without compromising patient safety. Achieving timely intervention requires addressing systemic delays—especially staffing and surgical capacity—through hospital-level improvements and policy support. Multidisciplinary coordination, designated trauma rooms, and orthogeriatric care have proven effective in streamlining processes and improving outcomes. Fracture-specific guidance for trochanteric fractures could enhance current hip fracture protocols. While implementing a < 24-hour surgery target poses challenges, doing so benefits both patients and healthcare systems. Known evidence Demographics and baseline-outcome The typical patient in our study was an elderly woman with chronic comorbidities, reflecting a 3:1 female-to-male ratio consistent with existing literature [ , , , – ]. Our in-hospital mortality rate for trochanteric femur fractures was 3.4%, slightly above the 2.6% national average for all hip fractures in Switzerland but well within the international range of 1.9-7.0.0% for trochanteric fractures [ , , , , – ]. Reported in-house complication rates globally vary between 12 and 46% [ , , – , ]. Early surgery benefits for patients with hip fractures generally Multiple studies support early surgery (within 24 h) for patients with hip fractures, showing reduced 30-day and one-year mortality, especially in elderly patients without reversible contraindications. Welford et al.’s 2021 meta-analysis of 46 studies confirmed these findings (RR 0.86), even when comparing to a 24–36 h window [ ]. Earlier meta-analyses reported significantly fewer complications with surgery within 24 h, yet significant mortality benefits appearing only at one-year postoperatively [ , ]. Patients with comorbidities seem to benefit most of early surgery [ , ]. The Hip Fracture Accelerated Surgical Treatment and Care Track (HIP ATTACK) RCT found no additional advantage of surgery within 6 h versus 24 h for complications or mortality but did show quicker mobilization and shorter hospital stay [ ]. While medical optimization of patients with severe and reversible conditions is crucial and guidelines exist, surgical delays in comorbid patients were also shown to reflect capacity challenges [ , ]. The Hip Fracture Accelerated Surgical Treatment and Care Track (HIP ATTACK) RCT found no additional advantage of surgery within 6 h versus 24 h for complications or mortality but did show quicker mobilization and shorter hospital stay [ ]. While medical optimization of patients with severe and reversible conditions is crucial and guidelines exist, surgical delays in comorbid patients were also shown to reflect capacity challenges [ , ]. Comparison with other studies Several studies support an association between surgical delays beyond 24 h and increased complication rates in trochanteric femur fractures. Daginnus et al. found this effect in Germany, but only for trochanteric – not femoral neck – fractures [ ]. Tanaka et al. observed similar results in Japan, albeit assessing a 48-hour-threshold for surgery [ ]. Vidan et al. reported the highest reported complication rate of 46% in acute hip surgery in Spain with a median delay of 72 h, largely due to operating room limitations [ ]. Pincus et al., in a Canadian study of 42,000 patients, identified 24 h as a key threshold for increased complications and 30-day mortality, though without fracture type differentiation [ ]. In a Swedish register analysis, Greve et al. linked delays over 24 h to worse outcomes, particularly in higher-risk patients [ASA III/IV and women] [ , ]. Other studies, such those by Delaveau [ ] and Schermann [ ], reinforce mortality benefits for surgery within 24 h, especially in the elderly. However, some studies like those by Tanner [ ], Orosz [ ], and Saul [ ] show mixed or minimal effects, likely due to small sample size, short delays, or heterogenous patient population. New contributions and strength of the study Despite extensive research upon acute hip fracture, many studies fail to differentiate between femoral neck and trochanteric fractures - two distinct entities which differ in pathophysiology, treatment, and outcomes [ , , , , ]. In trochanteric fractures, the lack of capsular confinement facilitates uncontained bleeding, soft tissue injury, inflammatory response, and are linked to higher complication and mortality rates, especially in older, frailer patients [ – ]. As the population ages, the incidence of trochanteric fractures is rising, particularly among men, making them increasingly relevant [ ]. Our study focuses specially on trochanteric fractures, confirming the association between surgical delay beyond 24 h and worse in-hospital outcome, while nighttime surgery was not found to be a risk factor. Closed reduction and intramedullary nailing, the standard treatment, is minimally invasive, resource-efficient, and manageable even by junior surgeons [ , ]. Avoiding night surgery due to staffing or logistical concerns contributes unnecessarily to surgical delay [ , , , , , , ]. While perceptions of nighttime risk persist, evidence from our study and others does not support increased harm in timely off-hour hip operations [ – ]. The large, multi-center cohort of over 7,000 patients strengthens the generalizability of our findings and underscores the need for fracture-specific guidelines - particularly as demographic shifts point to a growing burden of trochanteric fractures in aging populations [ ]. Limitations This study is limited trochanteric fractures treated with closed reduction and internal fixation; thus, findings cannot be generalized to complex cases or other procedures. Its retrospective design restricts causal inference, and stratifying solely by time to surgery may overlook necessary delay for medical optimization. Furthermore, procedural developments regarding surgical technique or management might have occurred over the 24 years observed. Registry-based analysis lacks detailed patient-level data, raising the risk of unmeasured confounding (e.g. reason for delay, hospital specific protocols, preoperative management). The AQC registry does not assess subdivisions of fracture or fixation type, neither orthogeriatric treatment, denying further analysis. No adjustments or propensity matching were performed. Generalizability is limited to healthcare systems with similar structures, and outcomes were restricted to the in-hospital period. Conclusion Minimizing surgical delays in trochanteric fractures is crucial, as unwarranted postponement increases the risk for adverse outcomes (complications, mortality) and costs without proven benefit. Night-time surgery was not associated with higher perioperative risk. While short delays for medical optimization may be justified, organizational improvements and orthogeriatric co-management are essential to ensure timely, safe surgery. With the rising incidence of fragility fractures, focused research and early multidisciplinary care remains key to improving outcomes and healthcare efficiency.

chunks.content: Introduction Background {6a} Gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy is a widely applied procedure for screening and treating upper GI diseases, particularly upper GI tumors. However, undergoing endoscopy without anesthesia may cause discomfort, nausea, vomiting, and even asphyxia [ ]. With advancements in anesthetic techniques, sedation has been increasingly used for GI endoscopy. Given the current situation, the number of sedated GI endoscopy procedures in China is expected to increase to 30 million in 2030. Patient safety during sedation for GI endoscopy is particularly important. Despite the application of oxygen supplementation using nasal cannulas, hypoxia continues to be one of the most common complications. Its incidence has been reported to range between 1.8% and 69% [ – ]. Insufficient ventilation caused by either hypoventilation or airway obstruction during deep sedation contributes to the occurrence of hypoxia. Long-term hypoxia can lead to coronary ischemia and permanent neurological damage, potentially leading to death [ ]. Relaxation of the upper airway muscles and increased susceptibility to airway collapse are unavoidable consequences of intravenous anesthesia. The main cause of hypoxia is upper airway obstruction caused by posterior displacement of the tongue [ , ]. Despite the advancements in methods for maintaining airway patency and preventing hypoxia during sedated endoscopy, such as jaw thrust as well as nasopharyngeal and oropharyngeal airway insertions, notable limitations remain. Previous studies have shown that lifting the patient’s jaw in the lateral position is insufficient [ ] and labor-intensive for healthcare providers. Furthermore, nasopharyngeal airway insertion increases the risk for nasal bleeding, whereas oropharyngeal airways can interfere with endoscope insertion. To maintain airway patency and oxygenation, Professor Diansan Su invented the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway, which was comprehensively introduced in our previous letter [ ]. The advantages of the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway include enhanced oxygenation, capnography, and endoscope navigation; reduced airway obstruction, particularly in patients with obesity; and provision of supraglottic jet ventilation. Our preliminary validation revealed that the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway can significantly reduce the incidence of hypoxia. Nevertheless, suboptimal sedation may lead to nausea and increased oral secretions during the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway implantation process, thereby affecting endoscopic procedures and even increasing the risk of airway accidents. Therefore, the device requires a relatively proper depth of sedation. On top of that,it remains to be validated by large-scale multicenter clinical studies. Thus, this study aims to evaluate the clinical efficiency of the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway in sedated esophagogastroduodenoscopy. We hypothesize that the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway can reduce the incidence of hypoxia in patients undergoing endoscopy. Objectives {7} This study aims to determine whether the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway can reduce the incidence of hypoxia in patients undergoing GI endoscopy under propofol sedation. Primary objective Our primary objective is to determine the incidence of hypoxia (75% ≤ SpO 2 < 90% for < 60 s). Secondary objective Our secondary objective is to determine the incidence rate of subclinical hypoxia (90% ≤ SpO 2 < 95%); severe hypoxia (SpO 2 < 75% or 75% ≤ SpO 2 < 90% for ≥ 60 s); and other adverse events (AEs), which are tools proposed by the International Sedation Task Force established by the World Society of Intravenous Anesthesia. Hyphothesis {7} We hypothesize that the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway will reduce hypoxia incidence for patients undergoing GI endoscopy with sedation. Our aim is to provide credible evidence regarding the enhancement of patient safety during GI endoscopy procedures. Trial design {8} This multicenter, randomized, open-label, two-arm parallel-group interventional superiority clinical trial aims to assess the effects of the intervention. The patients will be randomly divided into two groups in a 1:1 ratio. For each selected patient, researchers will determine their grouping through a central randomization system, but patients will not be informed of their grouping. This trial will be conducted in accordance with the Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials (SPIRIT). The trial was registered in ClinicalTrials.gov (No. NCT06081647 ) on October 15, 2023. Interventions Explanation for the selection of comparators {6b} The control group (Arm 1) will receive a conventional nasal cannula with capnography monitoring, which represents the current standard of care for oxygenation and ventilation monitoring during sedated gastrointestinal endoscopy in most clinical settings according to the guidelines. This comparator was selected for several scientific reasons. Firstly, the nasal cannula is widely used in clinical practice for oxygen delivery during procedural sedation and allows for direct comparison with the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway. By using the conventional nasal cannula as the comparator, we can objectively evaluate whether the COMBO device provides superior efficacy in preventing hypoxia without introducing confounding factors from unproven or non-standard devices. Secondly, hypoxia remains a common adverse event despite the use of nasal cannulas, highlighting a persistent clinical need. Comparing the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway against this established method will help determine whether it offers meaningful improvement in airway management. Intervention description {11a} Arms 1 and 2 will constitute the interventions in this trial.Control Group (Arm 1) will receive a standard endoscopy bite block to prevent biting the endoscope, along with a nasal cannula equipped with a CO 2 sampling port. Oxygen will be supplied at a flow rate of 3–4 L/min via the nasal cannula, with continuous monitoring of inhaled and exhaled CO 2 . Intervention Group (Arm 2) will receive the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway, an integrated device that combines the functions of a bite block, oxygen supply, and CO 2 sampling. The COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway provides an extra-oral oxygen delivery channel in addition to the nasal route, achieving dual-channel ventilation. Oxygen will be supplied at a total flow rate of 3–4 L/min, delivered through the nasal part of the device, consistent with the control group to ensure comparability. Sedation protocol In both groups, the following standardized sedation protocol will be applied: Administered for 1 min before the initiation of sedation. Then, Sufentanil 7 µg will be administered intravenously at the start of preoxygenation. After approximately 1 min of oxygen administration, propofol sedation will be initiated with an intravenous bolus of 1.5 mg/kg. Once a Ramsay Sedation Score of 5 or higher is achieved, the endoscopist will insert the endoscope and commence the procedure. Additional propofol boluses of 0.2–0.5 mg/kg will be intermittently administered as needed to maintain a Ramsay Sedation Score ≥ 5 throughout the examination. Timing The assigned intervention device (standard nasal cannula and bite block for Arm 1, or the bite block of the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway for Arm 2) will be placed and oxygen flow initiated immediately at the start of the preoxygenation period, which begins 1 min before the administration of propofol. The airway part of the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway will be immediately inserted after the patient’s Ramsay Sedation score reaches 5 or above. Sample size {14} According to the preliminary trial results and related literature, this study will use the PASS 15.0 software (two independent proportions, Fisher’s exact test) to estimate the sample size based on the difference in the incidence of hypoxia (75% ≤ SpO 2 < 90%, < 60 s) between Arms 1 and 2. Previous studies have reported that the incidence of hypoxia in patients in whom a conventional nasal cannula was used during painless gastroenterological endoscopy was approximately 8% [ ]. The parameters will be set as α = 0.05 and power = 0.8, with an expected reduction in hypoxia incidence from 8% to 4% and a dropout rate of 10%. The determined sample size is 1200 participants, randomly allocated in a ratio of 1:1, with 600 cases in Arm 1 and 600 in Arm 2. This multicenter study will enroll cases across centers on a competitive basis without a specific case number limit for each center. Recruitment {15} Achieving the target sample size of 1200 participants is anticipated to be feasible, given the vast volume of patients undergoing gastrointestinal endoscopy at the ten participating tertiary university hospitals across China. To ensure efficient and timely recruitment, we will implement the following active, multi-faceted strategy: A dedicated research coordinator at each site will proactively review the daily schedules of the gastrointestinal endoscopy centers to identify patients scheduled for procedures under propofol sedation. This allows for the early identification of a large pool of potential participants. Trained anesthesiologists or research staff will actively engage potential participants and their families, providing a clear and comprehensive explanation of the trial using standardized recruitment materials (e.g., brochures, posters). The communication will emphasize the following: (a) The potential benefit of receiving a novel device designed to reduce the risk of hypoxia, a common and concerning complication. (b) The safety of the intervention, explaining that it is integrated into the standard of care and does not alter the primary diagnostic or therapeutic procedure. Statistical methods Statistical methods for primary and secondary outcomes {20a} Data selection for statistical analysis Full analysis set (FAS): Following the intention-to-treat (ITT) approach, the FAS will include each participant who is randomized into the study and will receive the assigned treatment. The FAS will serve as the primary analysis set for all efficacy evaluations. Per-protocol set (PPS): The PPS will consist of FAS participants without major protocol deviations that could influence the assessment of primary outcomes. Such deviations may involve inconsistent sufentanil doses during the induction phase or a lack of primary outcome data. Efficacy evaluations will be conducted using the FAS and PPS datasets. Safety analysis set (SAS): The SAS will consist of all participants who will undergo the study treatment. Safety data analysis will be conducted exclusively on this group. Statistical methodology The statistical analysis plan will be developed before the trial concludes and finalized prior to database lock. It will include descriptive statistics and analytical methods. All statistical tests will be two-tailed and conducted using SPSS 23 (IBM, Armonk, NY). Furthermore, patient information will be expressed as mean ± standard deviation. Descriptive statistics for quantitative indicators will include the mean, standard deviation, median, minimum, and maximum values. Categorical variables will be expressed as numbers and percentages. The chi-squared tests will be employed to compare the incidence rates of hypoxia and AEs across the groups. Primary and secondary endpoints: These endpoints will be expressed as frequencies (incidence rates). Since the stratified block randomization by center ensures balance between groups within each center, the primary analysis for categorical outcomes will be performed using the Chi-squared tests without adjustment for center, as the randomization effectively controls for potential center effects. Moreover, we will also apply Fisher’s exact test where appropriate. A P -value < 0.05 will be considered statistically significant, with a 95% confidence interval. Postoperative adverse reactions (delirium, nasal congestion, nausea, and vomiting): These will be described using the number and percentage of cases. The incidence rates of adverse events will be compared using the chi-squared tests or Fisher’s exact probability test. For continuous outcomes, such as total propofol dose and procedure duration, we will use Student’s t -test for normally distributed data or the Mann-Whitney U test for non-normally distributed data. Additional analyses {20b} The overall safety assessment will focus on AE frequency and classification. Safety-related variables from all participants in the SAS will be organized into tables and presented accordingly. Categorization of AEs will be performed using the standardized terminology developed by the International Working Party on Sedation under the World Intravenous Anesthesia Society. The proportion of participants who will experience at least one AE will be analyzed using appropriate statistical methods, such as the chi-squared test, chi-squared test with continuity correction, or Fisher’s exact test, depending on the data distribution. Interim analyzes {21b} No formal interim analysis for efficacy or futility is planned for this trial. Discussion This study will be the first randomized controlled trial to systematically evaluate the impact of the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway on the reduction of hypoxia incidence in patients undergoing sedated GI endoscopy. Sedation for GI endoscopy has been increasingly applied worldwide. Ensuring patient safety during sedation for GI endoscopy is crucial. Hypoxia continues to be the most significant concern among patients undergoing GI endoscopy under propofol sedation [ , ]. Severe or persistent hypoxia often requires airway interventions, which may increase the risk for sedation-related AEs, such as hypotension, respiratory depression, and delayed recovery [ ]. Thus, maintaining oxygenation is crucial during sedated GI endoscopy. Several studies have investigated various methods to reduce the incidence of hypoxia during sedated GI endoscopy, including capnography [ ], supplemental oxygen [ ], different sedative agents [ ], and other ventilation techniques [ ]. However, none of them can effectively address the problem of airway patency. The COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway is a novel device that combines real-time monitoring of ventilation status through capnography and a direct mechanical intervention to maintain airway patency, which may be an effective adjunct to existing monitoring strategies, further enhancing patient safety during endoscopy procedures. Our study will be the first multicenter, randomized clinical trial to systematically evaluate the impact of the COMBO endoscopy oropharyngeal airway on hypoxia during GI endoscopy under propofol sedation. Our study is expected to provide high-quality evidence and improve the safety of sedated GI endoscopy. Nevertheless, our study has several limitations. First, it is an open-label clinical study, which may introduce potential bias. Second, it is not international; it only includes tertiary general hospitals in China, where sedative drugs or methods may differ across different institutions and countries. Third, we include only patients with normal body weight (18.5 < BMI < 30); thus, the effectiveness of airway management in patients who are overweight was not determined. We have planned a targeted study focusing on overweight patients in our future research. Our study has important clinical implications for managing patients undergoing GI endoscopy under propofol sedation.
